## 1. Morphology

### Hello

Welcome to _remorphable_.

Through this interactive web experience, you will get an introduction to morphology, one of the many fascinating branches of linguistics. You will learn about some of the basic concepts in morphology, including morphemes, lexemes, allomorphy, inflection, derivation, and more. ### What exactly is morphology?

Let's say we have the following (imaginary) English word:

**splinch** _verb_  
/splɪntʃ/ _what is this?_ ![Volume with solid fill](data:image/png;base64,)  
to step on broken glass

Try to use this word in the following sentence:

Interactive demo start

Last night, the clumsy burglar \_**\_**\_\_ on a broken window pane, leaving a trail of bloody footprints across the floor.

Interactive demo end; Hide next content until user enters a string that includes "splinch"

If you entered **"splinched"**, then this demonstrates that you have an intuitive knowledge of how to form new words in English, even if you have never used or heard of them before. We never defined the past tense of "splinch" as "splinched," and yet you inferred that adding the suffix "-ed" to the word would change its form and make it appropriate to use in this sentence.

How did you know that adding "-ed" has this effect? In fact, what other rules and techniques exist that help you modify words to convey different meanings? _How exactly are words formed?_

Morphology is the branch of linguistics that deals with this sort of thing. It is **the study of word formation**.

**morphology** _noun_  
/mɔɹˈfɑ.lə.dʒi/ ![Volume with solid fill](data:image/png;base64,)  
a study of structure and form; in linguistics, it is the study and description of word formation in language

## 2. Morphemes

### Morphemes

At the very core of morphology lies the concept of a **morpheme**.

**morpheme** _noun_  
/mɔːrfiːm/ ![Volume with solid fill](data:image/png;base64,)  
the smallest unit of language that **contains meaning**

Usually, this refers to the smaller components within a word that contribute to its meaning. In the previous "splinched" example, both "splinch" and "-ed" are individual morphemes that come together to form the past tense of "splinch."

Interactive demo start

Click on the word to separate it into its morphemes.

**unbreakable  
**impossible to break

After clicking

**un** **break** **able**  
not, opposite of separate into pieces capable of being

Interactive demo end; Hide next content until user separates the morphemes

Looks like that wasn't too impossible…

Morphemes can also be independent words themselves. Take the morpheme "break" for example—it can stand on its own, as well as join other morphemes to form a larger word. Such morphemes are called **free morphemes**.

The opposite of a free morpheme is a **bound morpheme**, which can only be part of a larger word and cannot stand on its own. In the example above, the prefix "un-" is a bound morpheme because it needs to attach to a base to modify its meaning, and it is not a valid word on its own.

Interactive demo start

Classify the following English morphemes into free and bound status.

un-, break, cat, the, -ness, -ful, quick, re-, -ing

**Free morphemes** **Bound morphemes**  
break, cat, the, quick un-, -ness, -ful, re-, -ing

Interactive demo end; Hide next content until user correctly classifies the morphemes

Great work!

Another way to classify morphemes is by their semantic attributes. In English words with multiple morphemes, we usually observe a **base** that contains the core meaning of the word, and **affixes** that attach to the base to modify its meaning.

In the "unbreakable" example, the morpheme "break" is a base, whereas "un-" and "-able" are affixes.

Affixes can be further categorized into **prefixes** and **suffixes**, where prefixes always attach to the start of the base, while suffixes always attach to the end. In our example, "un-" is a prefix, and "-able" is an affix.

## 3. 4. Inflection and derivation

### Is all word formation the same?

Let's look at the free morpheme "teach". If we attach the suffix "-er", we get "teacher". If we attach the suffix "-es", we get "teaches".

Are these two affixes doing the same kind of work?

Interactive demo start

Match each suffix to the linguistic function it is performing:

teach**es** Changes the core meaning and creates a completely new word (a noun)  
teach**er** Modifies the grammatical form of the existing verb

Interactive demo end; Hide next content until the user matches the forms correctly (criss-cross)

As you can see, affixes serve different purposes depending on how they interact with the base. This brings us to two major categories of affixation: **derivation** and **inflection**.

When an affix fundamentally changes the core meaning or the grammatical category (e.g. noun, adjective, adverb, etc.) of the base, this process is called **derivation**. Turning the _verb_ "teach" into the _noun_ "teacher" is a derivational process.

Conversely, when an affix attaches to a base merely to express a grammatical feature—such as tense (past/present/future) or quantity (single/dual/multiple)—without changing the word's underlying meaning or category, it is called **inflection**. Adding "-es" to "teach" simply gives us the third-person singular present tense of the exact same verb.

In a callout

Now that you have learnt about the two different categories of affixation, it is time to start building your conlang! **Click here** to open the conlang panel, where you can experiment with creating morphemes and fusing them to define words in your language.

## 5. Allomorphy

### Allomorphy

You're familiar with the English prefix "in-", which generally means "not" or "opposite of". Can we use this same prefix for all words where we need a negative counterpart?

Interactive demo start

Fill in the missing prefixes to create words that mean the opposite of the base:

\_\_+ tolerant = intolerant  
\_\_ + possible = ???  
\_\_ + legal = ???

Interactive demo end; Hide next content until user enters "in", "im", and "il"

Wait a minute, you used "im-" for impossible and "il-" for illegal! The prefix changed depending on its surrounding context. This phenomenon is known as **allomorphy**.

**allomorph** _noun_  
/ˈaləmɔːrf/ ![Volume with solid fill](data:image/png;base64,)  
any of the different variant forms of a single morpheme

Allomorphy occurs when a single morpheme has multiple **phonological variants**—called allomorphs—depending on the linguistic context surrounding it.

Why _phonological_? Because linguistics prioritizes the spoken form of language over its written realizations. Hence, there may even be allomorphs of a morpheme that are _spelt the same_ but _sound different_.

Interactive demo start

Select the exact sound that the plural "-s" or "-es" makes at the end of these words:

cats

/s/ (as in "snake")  
/z/ (as in "zoo")  
/ɪz/ (as in "is")

dogs

/s/ (as in "snake")  
/z/ (as in "zoo")  
/ɪz/ (as in "is")

buses

/s/ (as in "snake")  
/z/ (as in "zoo")  
/ɪz/ (as in "is")

Interactive demo end; Hide next content until user selects the correct sounds

The English plural suffix is the perfect example of a morpheme with multiple allomorphs, _including_ allomorphs with the same spelling but different pronunciations.

In a callout

Awesome stuff. You'll now see the different allomorphs of any morpheme that you locate in the English toolkit, and you'll also be able to create allomorphs in your conlang through the conlang panel!

## 6. Suppletion and lexemes

### What's up with "go" and "went"?

With allomorphy, we saw how an affix can take on different forms when it finds itself in different linguistic contexts. However, sometimes the addition of an affix completely changes the **base** of the word:

Interactive demo start

Enter the correct past tense form of each present tense verb:

**present past**

walk \_**\_\_  
teach \_**\_\_  
go \_\_\_\_\_

Interactive demo end; Hide next content until user enters "walked", "taught", and "went"

"Walked" makes perfect sense; it follows the standard rules of inflection. "Taught" is a bit quirky, but we can still sort of see the historical connection to "teach".

But there's not a single shared letter or sound between "go" and "went"!

**suppletion** _noun_  
/səˈpliːʃ(ə)n/ ![Volume with solid fill](data:image/png;base64,)  
when an inflected form of a word is completely phonologically unrelated to its base form

This morphological phenomenon is known as **suppletion**. It happens when a grammatical change (like changing the tense or making an adjective comparative) forces a word into a completely different form.

We also see this happen with the adjective "good". Turning it into its comparative counterpart changes the form to "better", which does _not_ share the same base as "good".

### Lexemes

So if "go" and "went" are completely different morphemes, how do we know that they're the "same" word? Or rather _different grammatical forms_ of the same word?

To solve this puzzle, linguists rely on the concept of a **lexeme**, which is an abstract unit of meaning that represents a complete set of _inflected_ word forms.

The lexeme go represents the core, abstract concept of moving from one place to another. "Go", "goes", "going", "gone", and "went" are not separate words but rather different word _forms_ belonging to the same underlying lexeme go.

We're able to link completely different phonetic sounds to the same core meaning because we store the abstract _lexeme_ in our heads. **Suppletion**, is therefore simply a scenario where a single lexeme is realized by word forms that sound nothing alike.

Interactive demo start

Drag the following word forms into the box of their correct lexeme:

am, mice, was, were, good, is, best, being, better, mouse, been

**be** **good** **mouse**  
am, was, were, is, being, been good, best, better mouse, mice

Interactive demo end; Hide next content until user sorts the word forms correctly

Exactly! Even though "am" and "was" look like total strangers, they are all simply different word forms of the same lexeme.

## 7. Conclusion

### Congratulations

You have reached the end of this web experience. You now know about some of the fundamental concepts of morphology, including morphemes, their basic classifications, and the phenomena of inflection, derivation, allomorphy, and suppletion!

But the journey doesn't end here! Morphology as a branch of linguistics is much, **much** larger than what we have covered on this website. We've discussed solutions to some of the easiest morphological problems that the English language presents, but indeed English can get much more complicated and irregular!

It doesn't stop at English either; the languages of the world have all sorts of different methods in which they form words, and you can learn more about these differences in the branch of **morphological typology**.

You can continue experimenting with the English toolkit or your own conlang as you wish. Once you feel like your conlang has reached a state where you are ready to share it with the world, press the &lt;TBD&gt; button near the top corner to generate a shareable poster that helps anyone learn your conlang in 10 minutes! ### Further reading

If you wish to keep learning about different morphology concepts, here are some good resources:

Lieber, R. (2016). _Introducing morphology_ (Second edition.). Cambridge University Press.

A concise and comprehensive introduction to morphology for students of linguistics. Covers a wide range of topics and serves as the primary source of information for this website.

Quinion, M. (2026). _Affixes: The building blocks of English_. Affixes.Org. <https://www.affixes.org/index.php>

A collection of affixes in the English language with their definitions and example usages. Useful if you would like to further explore the different affixes available in English.

Ramoo, D. (2021). 3.3 Morphology of different languages. _Psychologyoflanguage.Pressbooks.Tru.Ca_. <https://psychologyoflanguage.pressbooks.tru.ca/chapter/morphology-of-different-languages/>

This chapter from the online textbook "Psychology of Language" details the different ways in which languages can be classified based on their approach to word formation, and draws on examples from Turkish, Mandarin Chinese, Inuktitut, Arabic, and others. Check it out if you would like a quick intro to the morphologies of different languages of the world!
